models.title: 1. Social Media: Negative Impact on Individuals and Society
models.prompt: Many people believe that social networking sites have had a huge negative impact on both individuals and society. To what extent do you agree?
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — Band 9 model essay page
models.body:
Social networking platforms have transformed the way people communicate, obtain information and present themselves to others. Although these services offer obvious benefits, I largely agree that their widespread use has had damaging consequences for both individuals and society.

At an individual level, excessive use of social media can undermine mental well-being and distort people’s perception of ordinary life. Users are repeatedly exposed to carefully edited images of other people’s success, appearance and lifestyle, which can encourage unhealthy comparison. This is particularly problematic for teenagers, who may begin to measure their self-worth through likes, comments and online approval. In addition, the constant stream of notifications can fragment attention and make it harder to concentrate on study, work or face-to-face conversations.

The effects are also visible at a societal level. Social media algorithms tend to promote content that attracts strong reactions, meaning that sensational or divisive material can spread faster than balanced information. As a result, communities may become more polarised, while misinformation can influence public attitudes before it is properly verified. Furthermore, online interaction can sometimes replace rather than strengthen real-world relationships, leaving people surrounded by digital contacts but lacking meaningful social support.

This does not mean that social networking is inherently harmful. It can connect families across long distances, give small businesses access to customers and allow important social campaigns to reach large audiences. However, these advantages depend heavily on how responsibly the platforms are designed and used.

In conclusion, social media has considerable value, but its current form can damage attention, mental health and social cohesion. I therefore believe its overall impact is negative unless users and technology companies take greater responsibility for how it is used.

models.title: 2. Mobile Phones and Children
models.prompt: Some people think that mobile phones are harmful for children, while others disagree. Discuss both sides and give your opinion.
models.body:
Opinions differ over whether children should be allowed to use mobile phones. While these devices can expose young users to distraction and inappropriate content, I believe they can be beneficial when their use is limited and supervised.

Those who regard phones as harmful have several valid concerns. First, many applications are deliberately designed to hold users’ attention for as long as possible. Children, whose self-control is still developing, may therefore spend hours gaming, watching short videos or scrolling through social media instead of sleeping, exercising or studying. Excessive screen time can also reduce the quality of face-to-face interaction within families. A further concern is safety: unsupervised children may encounter cyberbullying, scams or material that is unsuitable for their age.

Nevertheless, mobile phones can also serve practical and educational purposes. Parents can contact their children in emergencies or track their location when they travel independently. Smartphones also provide instant access to dictionaries, educational videos, language-learning applications and school platforms. For older children in particular, learning to use digital tools responsibly is itself an important skill, since technology is embedded in higher education and modern employment.

In my view, the real issue is not the device itself but the absence of sensible boundaries. A child who is given unrestricted access to a phone is more likely to experience the disadvantages described above. By contrast, parents who set screen-time limits, restrict unsuitable applications and establish phone-free periods during meals or study can preserve most of the benefits while reducing the risks.

In conclusion, mobile phones can be harmful when used excessively or without supervision, but a complete ban is unnecessary. Managed carefully, they can be useful tools for safety, learning and communication.

models.title: 3. Advances in Air Travel
models.prompt: The advances in air travel are focused only in first class and this seems to have left others with no benefits at all. Do you agree or disagree?
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — Model IELTS Essay June 2020
models.body:
It is sometimes argued that innovation in air travel has benefited only first-class passengers. I disagree with this view because many of the most important improvements in aviation have affected all travellers, even if premium customers receive additional comforts.

The clearest advances have been in safety and efficiency. Modern aircraft are equipped with more reliable navigation systems, improved weather detection and increasingly sophisticated monitoring technology. These developments are not confined to expensive seats; every passenger on board benefits from a safer flight. Airlines have also become more efficient in areas such as online check-in, electronic boarding passes and automated baggage handling, all of which reduce delays and simplify the travel process for economy passengers as well.

There have also been substantial improvements in affordability and accessibility. The expansion of low-cost carriers has enabled millions of people to travel internationally who might previously have regarded flying as unaffordable. Competition between airlines has created a much wider range of fares and routes, while improvements in aircraft fuel efficiency have helped airlines operate long-distance services more economically. Economy passengers may not receive lie-flat seats or luxury lounges, but they benefit from a transport system that is broader, faster and more accessible than in the past.

Admittedly, some highly visible innovations are concentrated in business and first class. Private suites, premium meals and spacious seating are designed specifically for customers willing to pay considerably more. However, these are enhancements in comfort rather than the most significant advances in aviation itself.

In conclusion, first-class travel has undoubtedly become more luxurious, but it is inaccurate to claim that other passengers have gained nothing. Safety, convenience, route availability and lower-cost travel have improved the experience for the wider public.

models.title: 4. Global Warming: Causes and Solutions
models.prompt: Global warming is one of the biggest threats to our environment. What causes global warming? What solutions are there to this problem?
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — Environment Topic for Writing Task 2
models.body:
Global warming is largely the result of human activities that increase the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. The problem is global in scale, but a combination of government policy, technological change and individual action can significantly reduce its severity.

The principal cause is the burning of fossil fuels for electricity, transport and industry. Coal, oil and natural gas release large quantities of carbon dioxide, which traps heat in the atmosphere. Deforestation intensifies the problem because forests absorb carbon dioxide; when trees are removed, this natural carbon sink is weakened. Agriculture also contributes through methane emissions from livestock and certain farming practices. Taken together, these activities have made economic growth heavily dependent on carbon-intensive energy.

The most effective solution is therefore to reduce that dependence. Governments can accelerate investment in renewable energy, modernise electricity grids and establish stricter efficiency standards for buildings, vehicles and industry. Carbon pricing can also make polluting activities more expensive while encouraging cleaner alternatives. At the same time, protecting forests and restoring degraded land would increase the planet’s capacity to absorb carbon.

Individuals have a supporting role. Using public transport, reducing unnecessary flights, improving home energy efficiency and consuming fewer carbon-intensive products can lower personal emissions. However, individual choices are most effective when public infrastructure makes sustainable behaviour convenient and affordable. Asking people to drive less, for example, is unrealistic if reliable public transport does not exist.

In conclusion, global warming is driven mainly by fossil-fuel consumption, deforestation and high-emission agriculture. Meaningful progress requires structural changes led by governments and industry, reinforced by responsible consumer behaviour. No single measure will solve the problem, but coordinated action across these areas can substantially limit future warming.

models.title: 5. Who Should Be Responsible for Environmental Problems?
models.prompt: Some people think environmental problems should be dealt with by governments, while others believe individuals are responsible. Discuss both sides and give your opinion.
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — Environment Topic for Writing Task 2
models.body:
There is continuing debate over whether environmental protection is primarily a government responsibility or an individual one. Although personal behaviour matters, I believe governments must take the leading role because the largest environmental problems require regulation, infrastructure and coordination on a scale that individuals cannot provide.

Those who emphasise individual responsibility argue that environmental damage is ultimately caused by millions of everyday choices. Household energy use, private car travel, unnecessary consumption and poor waste disposal all contribute to pollution and resource depletion. If citizens recycle, conserve electricity and choose lower-emission transport, the cumulative effect can be substantial. Moreover, public demand can influence companies: businesses are more likely to adopt sustainable practices when consumers reward them for doing so.

However, individual action has clear limits. A commuter cannot choose an efficient railway system if the government has failed to build one, nor can a household prevent a factory from discharging pollutants into a river. National authorities can impose emissions standards, protect natural habitats, fund renewable-energy infrastructure and design tax systems that discourage environmentally damaging behaviour. They can also negotiate international agreements, which is essential for problems such as climate change that cross national borders.

In my view, the most realistic approach is shared responsibility with government leadership. Policy should create the conditions in which sustainable choices become easy, affordable and normal, while citizens should respond by adjusting their behaviour. Without public participation, environmental laws may be politically difficult to sustain; without effective policy, personal efforts are likely to remain fragmented.

In conclusion, individuals have an important part to play, but governments possess the authority and resources needed to produce change at scale. Environmental progress is therefore most likely when strong public policy and responsible personal behaviour reinforce one another.

models.title: 6. International Exchange Visits for Teenagers
models.prompt: Some educationalists think that international exchange visits will benefit teenagers at school. To what extent do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?
models.body:
International exchange programmes allow school students to live and study in another country for a limited period. Although such schemes can be expensive and emotionally demanding, I believe their educational and personal benefits generally outweigh these disadvantages.

The strongest advantage is that students gain forms of learning that are difficult to reproduce in a classroom. Living with a host family or attending a foreign school exposes teenagers to different customs, social expectations and ways of thinking. This can challenge stereotypes and develop cultural awareness at an age when attitudes are still being formed. Exchange visits can also accelerate language learning because students must use the language for genuine communication rather than only for exercises and examinations.

A second benefit is increased independence. Teenagers who are temporarily separated from their usual support network have to manage unfamiliar situations, communicate with new people and solve everyday problems for themselves. These experiences can strengthen confidence and adaptability, both of which are valuable later in higher education and employment.

There are, admittedly, disadvantages. The cost of travel and accommodation can exclude students from lower-income families unless schools provide financial support. Some participants may also experience homesickness, culture shock or disruption to their normal studies. However, these difficulties can be reduced through scholarships, careful selection of host families and academic planning before the exchange begins.

Overall, the disadvantages are practical problems that can largely be managed, whereas the advantages can influence a young person’s outlook for years. In conclusion, well-designed international exchange programmes provide meaningful academic, linguistic and personal development, and their benefits outweigh the potential drawbacks.

models.title: 7. Should Teenagers Study All Subjects?
models.prompt: Some people think teenagers should concentrate on all subjects at school. Others believe teenagers should focus on the subjects they are best at or most interested in. To what extent do you agree?
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — School Subjects model-essay page
models.body:
Whether teenagers should study a broad curriculum or specialise early is a question of educational priorities. I believe schools should maintain a reasonably broad core of subjects while allowing older students to devote more time to areas in which they show particular ability or interest.

A broad education is important because adolescents are not always in a position to make permanent academic choices. A fourteen-year-old who dislikes science, for example, may later discover an interest in medicine, engineering or environmental studies. Removing subjects too early could close off future pathways before students fully understand their own strengths. Core study in mathematics, language, science and the humanities also provides general knowledge and transferable skills that are useful regardless of career choice.

Nevertheless, requiring every student to spend equal time on every subject becomes inefficient as they grow older. Students differ substantially in aptitude and ambition. Someone with exceptional ability in mathematics may benefit more from advanced mathematics and programming than from additional compulsory art classes, while a talented musician may need time for performance and theory. Greater specialisation can therefore increase motivation and allow students to reach a higher level in the fields most relevant to their future.

The best system, in my view, is gradual specialisation rather than an abrupt choice between breadth and focus. Younger teenagers should study a wide range of subjects, but schools should progressively increase elective options during the final years of secondary education.

In conclusion, a common academic foundation protects students from narrowing their opportunities too early, while later specialisation recognises individual strengths and goals. Combining the two approaches is more educationally sound than insisting on either complete uniformity or complete freedom.

models.title: 8. Technology in the Workplace
models.prompt: Modern technology is now very common in most workplaces. How has this changed the way we work? Are there disadvantages to relying too much on technology?
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — Technology Topic for Writing Task 2
models.body:
Technology has fundamentally changed both where work is performed and how tasks are completed. While these developments have raised productivity and flexibility, excessive dependence on digital systems also creates significant risks.

One major change is the automation of routine work. Software can now process transactions, analyse large datasets and complete administrative tasks that once required substantial human labour. This allows employees to devote more time to judgement, creativity and problem-solving. Communication has also become less dependent on physical location. Video conferencing, cloud platforms and instant messaging enable teams to collaborate across cities and countries, while remote work has given many employees greater control over where they live and how they organise their day.

However, over-reliance on technology can make organisations vulnerable. A cyberattack, software failure or network outage can interrupt operations almost instantly when essential processes have no workable manual alternative. Heavy automation may also weaken employees’ underlying skills if people become accustomed to accepting computer-generated results without questioning them. In addition, constant digital connectivity can blur the boundary between work and private life, creating pressure to respond to messages outside normal working hours.

The sensible response is not to resist technology but to build resilience around it. Companies should maintain backup systems, train staff to understand rather than merely operate important tools, and establish clear expectations about after-hours communication.

In conclusion, technology has made work faster, more flexible and more internationally connected. Nevertheless, organisations that become completely dependent on digital systems may sacrifice resilience, human judgement and work-life boundaries. The greatest benefits therefore come from using technology as a powerful tool rather than treating it as a substitute for human capability.

models.title: 9. Does the Internet Bring People Closer or Make Them More Isolated?
models.prompt: An increasing number of people use the internet to meet new people and socialise. Some think this has brought people closer together while others think people are becoming more isolated. Discuss both sides and give your opinion.
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — Technology Topic for Writing Task 2
models.body:
The internet has created unprecedented opportunities for social interaction, yet there is disagreement over whether this strengthens relationships or contributes to isolation. In my view, online communication can bring people closer, but it becomes harmful when it replaces rather than complements face-to-face contact.

On the positive side, the internet removes geographical barriers. Families living in different countries can communicate regularly through video calls and messaging, while people with unusual interests or medical conditions can find communities that may not exist locally. Online platforms can also help shy individuals initiate friendships more easily because digital communication may feel less intimidating than approaching strangers in person. In these situations, technology expands a person’s social world.

On the other hand, the quantity of online interaction does not necessarily reflect its quality. Someone may exchange messages with hundreds of contacts while having very few people they can rely on in a crisis. Social media can encourage brief, low-effort communication and can create the illusion of connection without the emotional depth associated with close relationships. Furthermore, if online entertainment and communication occupy most of a person’s free time, opportunities for real-world interaction may gradually decline.

I therefore believe the effect depends on how the internet is used. When online tools maintain existing relationships or help people form connections that later develop offline, they can reduce isolation. When they become a substitute for direct human contact, they may have the opposite effect.

In conclusion, the internet is neither inherently connecting nor isolating. It is best understood as a communication tool whose social impact depends on whether it supports or displaces meaningful relationships.

models.title: 10. Why Do Criminals Reoffend?
models.prompt: Many criminals commit further crimes as soon as they are released from prison. What are the causes of this, and what solutions can you suggest?
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — Crime & Punishment Essay Titles
models.body:
High rates of reoffending are a serious problem because imprisonment is of limited value if former offenders quickly return to crime. Recidivism is often driven by poor reintegration, limited employment prospects and unresolved personal problems, and these factors can be addressed through rehabilitation and structured support after release.

One major cause is the difficulty ex-prisoners face in finding legitimate work. A criminal record can make employers reluctant to hire them, while some prisoners leave custody with few qualifications or marketable skills. Without a stable income, returning to illegal activity may appear to be the easiest way to survive. Another factor is that prisons do not always address the causes behind offending, such as drug dependence, poor mental health or violent behaviour. Finally, former prisoners may return to the same social environment and peer group that contributed to their original crime.

A more effective system would therefore focus on rehabilitation before release and reintegration afterwards. Prisons should provide vocational training, literacy education, addiction treatment and psychological support according to individual needs. Governments could also create incentives for employers to hire suitable former offenders, reducing the barrier created by a criminal record. Equally important, probation services should help people secure housing, employment and access to treatment during the first months after release, when the risk of reoffending is particularly high.

Punishment remains necessary, especially for serious offences, but it should not be the only objective of the justice system. If prison merely removes offenders from society temporarily without changing the conditions that contributed to their behaviour, repeated crime is predictable.

In conclusion, reoffending is largely caused by weak rehabilitation and difficult social reintegration. Combining punishment with education, treatment and post-release support offers a more realistic way to reduce repeat crime.

models.title: 11. Obesity as a Growing Global Problem
models.prompt: Obesity is a growing problem around the world. Why is this happening, and what can be done about it?
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — Writing Task 2 Essay Topics 2024
models.body:
Rising obesity rates are the result of an environment in which high-calorie food is widely available while everyday life requires less physical activity than in the past. Because the causes are both behavioural and structural, effective solutions must make healthy choices easier rather than relying solely on individual willpower.

Diet is a central factor. Highly processed foods are often cheap, convenient and aggressively marketed, whereas healthier options may require more time to prepare and can be more expensive in some communities. Portion sizes have also increased, making excessive calorie intake seem normal. At the same time, many occupations are sedentary, urban travel is dominated by cars, and entertainment increasingly takes place on screens. People can therefore go through an entire day while expending very little physical energy.

Governments can respond in several ways. Clear food labelling and restrictions on advertising unhealthy products to children would help consumers make more informed choices. Urban planning should prioritise safe walking routes, cycling infrastructure and accessible public recreation facilities so that physical activity becomes part of daily life. Schools can contribute by providing nutritious meals and regular physical education. Healthcare systems should also identify people at risk early and provide evidence-based weight-management support rather than waiting until obesity-related diseases develop.

Individuals still have responsibility for their diet and activity levels, but personal responsibility operates within the environment people inhabit. Advice to “eat less and move more” is unlikely to be sufficient if unhealthy food is cheaper, neighbourhoods are difficult to walk in and working hours leave little time for exercise.

In conclusion, obesity is increasing because modern food systems encourage overconsumption while lifestyles reduce movement. Lasting progress will require coordinated changes in public policy, education, healthcare and personal habits.

models.title: 12. Encouraging Adults to Exercise
models.prompt: Some people think showing major sports events on television is the best way to encourage adults to exercise. Others believe there are more effective ways. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — School Subjects page (additional reported questions)
models.body:
Major sporting events can inspire people to become more active, but I do not believe television coverage is the most effective way to increase exercise among adults. Inspiration has value, yet practical barriers such as time, cost and access usually determine whether people exercise regularly.

Supporters of televised sport argue that elite athletes provide visible examples of fitness, discipline and achievement. Events such as the Olympics can generate enthusiasm for activities that viewers might not otherwise consider. A person who watches a successful swimming or cycling event, for instance, may feel motivated to try the sport personally. Broadcasting also reaches millions of people at relatively low cost, making it an efficient way to promote the idea of an active lifestyle.

However, motivation created by a sporting event can be short-lived. Adults who work long hours, live far from sports facilities or cannot afford membership fees may still remain inactive. More effective measures would remove these practical obstacles. Employers could provide flexible time for exercise, local authorities could build safe walking and cycling routes, and communities could offer inexpensive fitness programmes. Public-health campaigns could also encourage achievable forms of activity, such as brisk walking, rather than presenting exercise only through elite competition.

In my opinion, televised sport is useful as a source of inspiration, but it should form only one part of a broader strategy. People are more likely to exercise consistently when physical activity is convenient, affordable and compatible with everyday routines.

In conclusion, sports broadcasting can encourage some adults, but improving access and reducing practical barriers is a more reliable way to create lasting behaviour change.

models.title: 13. Seeking Medical Advice Online
models.prompt: Some people use technology to seek advice for medical problems rather than seeing a doctor. Why is this happening, and is it a positive or negative development?
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — School Subjects page (additional reported questions)
models.body:
Increasing numbers of people search online or use digital services for medical advice before consulting a doctor. This trend is mainly driven by convenience, cost and immediate access to information. In my view, it is positive when technology supports professional care, but negative when online information is treated as a substitute for proper diagnosis.

The attraction of digital health information is easy to understand. Booking a medical appointment may involve waiting several days, taking time off work or travelling to a clinic, whereas a search engine or health application can provide information within seconds. Online resources may also help people understand unfamiliar symptoms, learn about treatment options or decide whether a problem requires urgent attention. Telemedicine can be particularly valuable for people in remote areas who have limited access to specialists.

The danger is that medical information is highly dependent on context. The same symptom can have many different causes, and people without medical training may misinterpret what they read. Online content also varies greatly in reliability; commercially motivated websites and social-media posts can present unproven treatments as if they were established medicine. This may lead people to delay appropriate care, take unsuitable medication or become unnecessarily anxious about minor symptoms.

For these reasons, technology should be used as a gateway to healthcare rather than a replacement for it. Reputable services can provide general guidance, help patients prepare questions and make remote consultations easier, but diagnosis and treatment decisions should remain grounded in qualified medical assessment when the condition is significant or uncertain.

In conclusion, the growth of online medical advice reflects genuine problems of access and convenience. It is beneficial as an additional source of support, but potentially harmful when users rely on it instead of professional evaluation.

models.title: 14. Public Parks versus Housing and Business Development
models.prompt: Some people think public parks should be used for housing or business development because urban land is limited. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — Environment Topic for Writing Task 2
models.body:
As cities grow, pressure on urban land inevitably increases, leading some people to argue that public parks should be converted into housing or commercial space. I disagree with this approach because green spaces provide essential public benefits that are difficult and costly to replace once they are lost.

The strongest argument for redevelopment is the urgent need for housing. In cities with rapidly rising populations, limited supply can push rents and property prices beyond the reach of ordinary residents. Commercial development can also create jobs and increase local tax revenue. From this perspective, large parks in valuable central locations may appear to be an inefficient use of scarce land.

However, this calculation ignores the services that urban green spaces provide. Parks give residents free access to exercise, recreation and contact with nature, which is particularly important for people who live in small apartments and cannot afford private facilities. Trees and vegetation also reduce urban heat, absorb some air pollution and help manage rainwater. In densely built neighbourhoods, these environmental functions can directly improve public health and make cities more resilient to extreme weather.

Moreover, destroying parks is not the only way to increase housing supply. Governments can encourage higher-density construction around transport hubs, redevelop abandoned industrial land and convert underused commercial buildings into homes. These approaches make better use of existing urban space without sacrificing public assets that benefit the entire community.

In conclusion, the shortage of housing and commercial land is a legitimate concern, but converting parks is a short-sighted solution. Cities should increase density and reuse poorly utilised land while protecting green spaces as essential infrastructure rather than treating them as empty land awaiting development.

models.title: 15. What Is the Function of Schools?
models.prompt: Some people think schools merely turn children into good citizens and workers rather than benefiting them as individuals. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
models.promptSource: IELTS Liz — The Function of Schools
models.body:
Schools undeniably prepare young people to participate in society and employment, but it is too narrow to suggest that this is their only function. I believe a good education serves both social needs and individual development, and these aims are often mutually reinforcing rather than contradictory.

Schools do help create capable citizens and workers. Students learn literacy, numeracy and subject knowledge that later allow them to contribute economically. They also learn to follow rules, cooperate with others, meet deadlines and resolve disagreements, all of which are essential in workplaces and communities. From a societal perspective, education also passes on shared knowledge and civic principles that help people participate in public life.

Yet the same institutions can benefit children in deeply personal ways. Exposure to literature, science, sport, music and other subjects allows students to discover interests and abilities they may not encounter at home. Supportive teachers can help a child develop confidence, curiosity and the ability to think independently. Schools also bring young people into contact with peers from different backgrounds, giving them opportunities to form friendships and understand perspectives beyond their own family environment.

Indeed, personal development and social preparation are not competing goals. A student who becomes more confident and intellectually independent is also likely to become a more adaptable employee and engaged citizen. Similarly, learning to cooperate benefits both the individual and the wider community.

In conclusion, schools certainly prepare children for adult responsibilities, but reducing education to the production of workers and obedient citizens misunderstands its broader purpose. The most successful schools equip students to contribute to society while also helping them develop their own interests, judgement and potential.
